issues.description:
** The VS Code pointer path is knowingly wired to a black-frame backend and its required artifact proof fails.
  - **Category:** Correctness / Completeness
  - **Severity:** Major
  - **Evidence paths:** `tools/dabbler-ai-orchestration/scripts/obs-capture.js`, `tools/dabbler-ai-orchestration/scripts/record-vscode-walkthrough.js`, `tools/dabbler-ai-orchestration/scripts/pointer.js`, `docs/session-sets/113-narrated-video-walkthroughs/s7-pointer-visibility-vscode.json`, `docs/session-sets/113-narrated-video-walkthroughs/s7-cursor-capture-backends.json`
  - **Failure scenario:** Every VS Code run requesting `physicalPointer` sets `needCursorVisible`, which unconditionally selects BitBlt. The committed backend measurement says BitBlt black-frames Electron, and the committed visibility result is `FAIL`. This is the main VS Code recording path, so cursor-enabled recordings will probably contain unusable frames or no visible pointer rather than the promised workbench-plus-pointer.
  - **Acceptance criterion:** `JUDGMENT - A recording made through the supported VS Code recorder must show both a real non-development-host VS Code window and the moving pointer at every click target, its feature-off control must fail the same pixel check, and pointer/backend unavailability must prevent an apparently successful cursor-enabled recording.`
  - **Details:** **Violation:** The plan requires the physical pointer to be visible in recorded frames and ends with “every recording this framework makes shows a pointer that moves.” **Impact:** The primary Windows recording path cannot produce the promised tutorial artifact; merging it would bless a mode already measured to fail. **Evidence:** `ObsCaptureSession.configure()` selects `CAPTURE_METHOD_BITBLT` whenever `needCursorVisible` is true; `record-vscode-walkthrough.js` sets that option for both pointer and control runs; the backend report records `windowPresent: false` for BitBlt; and the VS Code visibility artifact records zero passed probes and verdict `FAIL`. The correct result is a supported, fully evaluated backend or equivalent capture method that produces both window and cursor, with cursor-enabled runs failing closed when that cannot be achieved.
issues.failureScenario: Every VS Code run requesting `physicalPointer` sets `needCursorVisible`, which unconditionally selects BitBlt. The committed backend measurement says BitBlt black-frames Electron, and the committed visibility result is `FAIL`. This is the main VS Code recording path, so cursor-enabled recordings will probably contain unusable frames or no visible pointer rather than the promised workbench-plus-pointer.

acceptance.statement: A recording made through the supported VS Code recorder must show both a real non-development-host VS Code window and the moving pointer at every click target, its feature-off control must fail the same pixel check, and pointer/backend unavailability must prevent an apparently successful cursor-enabled recording.

issues.description:
** The pointer visibility checker can pass without proving that a cursor is visible at every click.
  - **Category:** Correctness / False Positive
  - **Severity:** Major
  - **Evidence paths:** `tools/dabbler-ai-orchestration/scripts/check-pointer-visible.js`, `tools/dabbler-ai-orchestration/scripts/record-vscode-walkthrough.js`, `docs/session-sets/113-narrated-video-walkthroughs/s7-pointer-visibility-vscode.json`
  - **Failure scenario:** Moving the real pointer over a typical VS Code tree row changes hover backgrounds or reveals row actions even when the capture backend omits the cursor. The checker only asks whether “something” changed in the target crop while one unrelated control crop stayed still, so ordinary hover rendering can satisfy the cursor test. It also returns `PASSED` when any probe passes and the remaining probes are `indecisive`; nearby successive targets are common, and the committed VS Code run already produced two indecisive probes.
  - **Acceptance criterion:** `JUDGMENT - A cursor-hidden recording in which real mouse movement causes target hover changes must fail the visibility check, and an overall pass must require affirmative cursor evidence for every synthesized click rather than allowing indecisive probes.`
  - **Details:** **Violation:** The required proof is that “a pointer is visible in the recorded frames near the target’s bounding box at the moment of the click,” not merely that target pixels changed. **Impact:** The falsifier can certify a cursor-free recording, undermining the session’s load-bearing artifact proof. This is probable because hover effects are normal on interactive controls and repeated nearby targets already occur in the supplied scenario. **Evidence:** The pass branch tests only `targetChanged >= 0.03` and a static top-left control; its detail explicitly says “something appeared.” Final verdict logic allows `passed > 0`, `failed == 0`, and arbitrarily many `indecisive` probes to pass. The correct instrument must identify cursor-shaped/moving evidence or use a differential design that excludes hover changes, and it must not treat unverified clicks as successful.
issues.failureScenario: Moving the real pointer over a typical VS Code tree row changes hover backgrounds or reveals row actions even when the capture backend omits the cursor. The checker only asks whether “something” changed in the target crop while one unrelated control crop stayed still, so ordinary hover rendering can satisfy the cursor test. It also returns `PASSED` when any probe passes and the remaining probes are `indecisive`; nearby successive targets are common, and the committed VS Code run already produced two indecisive probes.

acceptance.statement: A cursor-hidden recording in which real mouse movement causes target hover changes must fail the visibility check, and an overall pass must require affirmative cursor evidence for every synthesized click rather than allowing indecisive probes.

issues.description:
** The required human-driven long-form capture harness was not built.
  - **Category:** Completeness
  - **Severity:** Major
  - **Evidence paths:** `tools/dabbler-ai-orchestration/scripts/record-vscode-walkthrough.js`, `tools/dabbler-ai-orchestration/scripts/measure-pointer-visibility.js`, `tools/dabbler-ai-orchestration/scripts/measure-cursor-capture-backends.js`, `docs/tutorials/single-module-walkthrough.md`
  - **Failure scenario:** An operator beginning a real shipped-product session has no harness that starts recording a normal VS Code window, waits while the human works, stops around session boundaries, and names the file by set/session. The only changed VS Code recorder still launches an Extension Development Host, creates a UAT workspace, and executes authored scenario mechanics, so a typical operator cannot make the required long-form recording without manually assembling unsupported commands.
  - **Acceptance criterion:** `JUDGMENT - The tree contains and documents an opt-in start/stop harness for a human-driven session in a normal VS Code window, names one recording by set and session, and demonstrably does not write lifecycle state or drive the orchestrator.`
  - **Details:** **Violation:** Step 3 requires capture “around a real session in a real VS Code window, not the Extension Development Host,” with the driver explicitly being a person. **Impact:** The core genre change has not been implemented, so the tutorial cannot be recorded through the framework. **Evidence:** `record-vscode-walkthrough.js` remains a Playwright scenario driver using `--extensionDevelopmentPath` and a generated UAT workspace; the new measurement scripts are expressly measurements rather than recorders. The correct fix is a separate observational human-session harness, not another scenario wrapper.

issues.description:
** The speed-ramp algorithm does not derive waiting intervals; it treats every unmarked gap as waiting.
  - **Category:** Correctness
  - **Severity:** Major
  - **Evidence paths:** `ai_router/speed_ramp.py`, `ai_router/tests/test_speed_ramp.py`, `docs/tutorials/single-module-walkthrough.md`
  - **Failure scenario:** During the intended human-driven tutorial, the operator reads, types, reviews AI output, or edits a plan between sparse lifecycle timestamps. `build_segments()` preserves only a three-second pad around each point mark and compresses the rest by up to 40×. Those active stretches are therefore likely to be sped through even though something happened, materially damaging the tutorial.
  - **Acceptance criterion:** `JUDGMENT - Given a representative human session record containing active intervals between lifecycle events, the generated plan must preserve those intervals at 1x and compress only intervals whose event semantics establish that the session was waiting.`
  - **Details:** **Violation:** The plan says waiting is “derivable” from the framework record and commands “never compress an interval where something happened.” **Impact:** The main tutorial workflow can compress the human work viewers need to see; manual advice to inspect the plan does not satisfy the promised derivation or invariant. **Evidence:** `build_segments()` constructs six-second keep regions around timestamp points and `_quiet_segments()` labels every remaining gap “nothing was recorded,” without interpreting start/end event types or activity durations. The tutorial itself admits that a person reading looks exactly like a running suite. The correct implementation must derive intervals from event semantics or collect explicit activity/wait boundaries rather than infer waiting solely from timestamp absence.

Those active stretches are therefore likely to be sped through even though something happened, materially damaging the tutorial.

acceptance.statement: Given a representative human session record containing active intervals between lifecycle events, the generated plan must preserve those intervals at 1x and compress only intervals whose event semantics establish that the session was waiting.

issues.description:
Enabling the physical pointer selects the backend already measured to black-frame VS Code

- **Category:** Correctness
- **Severity:** Major
- **Evidence paths:** `tools/dabbler-ai-orchestration/scripts/record-vscode-walkthrough.js`, `tools/dabbler-ai-orchestration/scripts/obs-capture.js`, `docs/session-sets/113-narrated-video-walkthroughs/s7-cursor-capture-backends.json`, `docs/session-sets/113-narrated-video-walkthroughs/s7-pointer-outcome.md`
- **Failure scenario:** Every VS Code run with `physicalPointer` sets `needCursorVisible: true`; `ObsCaptureSession.configure()` deterministically maps that to BitBlt. The committed measurement reports BitBlt's `windowCorrelation` as `0` and `windowPresent: false`, matching the known black-frame behavior of hardware-accelerated Electron. Thus a typical pointer-enabled recording loses the product UI entirely.
- **Acceptance criterion:** `JUDGMENT - A real Windows run with the physical-pointer option must record both the VS Code workbench and cursor, pass the artifact visibility check, and use a capture backend that has passed the applicable capture-pilot criteria.`
- **Details:** **Violation:** The session must “show the pointer” on the VS Code path, while the decision record claims “no backend was swapped.” **Impact:** The option intended to fix cursorless recordings instead produces a black recording, so the main feature is unusable and should block merge. **Evidence:** `record-vscode-walkthrough.js` passes `needCursorVisible` for both pointer and control runs; `obs-capture.js` selects `CAPTURE_METHOD_BITBLT` whenever that flag is true; the measurement says that backend does not contain the workbench. The correct fix is not to route production pointer captures through the known-black backend; use a backend proven to capture both UI and pointer, or keep the feature unavailable until one exists.

The committed measurement reports BitBlt's `windowCorrelation` as `0` and `windowPresent: false`, matching the known black-frame behavior of hardware-accelerated Electron. Thus a typical pointer-enabled recording loses the product UI entirely.

acceptance.statement: A real Windows run with the physical-pointer option must record both the VS Code workbench and cursor, pass the artifact visibility check, and use a capture backend that has passed the applicable capture-pilot criteria.

issues.description:
The speed-ramp treats every unmarked gap as waiting, so ordinary human work is compressed

- **Category:** Correctness
- **Severity:** Major
- **Evidence paths:** `ai_router/speed_ramp.py`, `ai_router/tests/test_speed_ramp.py`, `docs/tutorials/single-module-walkthrough.md`
- **Failure scenario:** In the required human-driven tutorial, the operator reads, types, edits files, and responds to AI between sparse lifecycle timestamps. `build_segments()` protects only a three-second pad around each instantaneous mark and compresses every sufficiently long gap, often at up to 40×. Human activity between those marks is therefore likely to become an unreadable fast-forward even though it was not waiting.
- **Acceptance criterion:** `JUDGMENT - Given a representative human session containing both an active-work interval and a bounded known-wait interval, the generated plan must leave the complete active interval at 1× and compress only the known wait.`
- **Details:** **Violation:** The requirement says waiting must be “derived from the framework's own record” and “never compress an interval where something happened.” **Impact:** The resulting tutorial can accelerate the very authoring and decomposition work it is supposed to demonstrate, materially defeating the tutorial objective. **Evidence:** The implementation does not interpret event types, pair start/end records, or identify wait states; `_quiet_segments()` is called for every gap between padded timestamps. Its tests establish only that no timestamp itself falls inside a compressed segment, not that active intervals remain uncompressed. The walkthrough even admits that reading and typing can look identical to waiting. The correct implementation must derive bounded wait intervals from event semantics or collect additional active-work evidence, rather than equating absence of timestamps with waiting.

Human activity between those marks is therefore likely to become an unreadable fast-forward even though it was not waiting.

acceptance.statement: Given a representative human session containing both an active-work interval and a bounded known-wait interval, the generated plan must leave the complete active interval at 1× and compress only the known wait.

issues.description:
The pixel checker can pass without proving that a cursor is visible

- **Category:** Correctness
- **Severity:** Major
- **Evidence paths:** `tools/dabbler-ai-orchestration/scripts/check-pointer-visible.js`, `tools/dabbler-ai-orchestration/scripts/record-vscode-walkthrough.js`, `tools/dabbler-ai-orchestration/scripts/measure-pointer-visibility.js`, `docs/session-sets/113-narrated-video-walkthroughs/s7-pointer-visibility-vscode.json`
- **Failure scenario:** Moving the real pointer onto a normal button or tree row changes that target's local hover styling even when the capture backend omits the cursor. The checker sees target-local change, sees no change in its unrelated top-left control crop, and reports a pass. Repeated or nearby targets also commonly become `indecisive`; the checker still returns `PASSED` if only one probe passes and all remaining probes are indecisive.
- **Acceptance criterion:** `JUDGMENT - A recording with no cursor pixels but a target-local hover change must fail, every required click must be conclusively measured before the run can pass, and frame timestamps must be synchronized from an actual recording-start/end anchor rather than an unrelated last event.`
- **Details:** **Violation:** The required proof is that “a pointer is visible in the recorded frames near the target's bounding box at the moment of the click.” **Impact:** The instrument can certify a cursorless artifact, making both its positive result and falsifier misleading. This directly undermines the load-bearing artifact proof. **Evidence:** The pass condition says only that “something appeared at the target”; it does not identify cursor pixels or distinguish local hover effects. Its final verdict ignores `indecisive` probes when there are no explicit failures. The committed VS Code run already contains two indecisive probes out of six, showing this is not hypothetical. Additionally, `recordingStartOffsetMillis()` assumes the final event coincides with the file's end without checking the event type or capture-stop boundary. The checker needs cursor-specific discrimination, conclusive coverage of every required action, and reliable clock alignment.
issues.failureScenario: Moving the real pointer onto a normal button or tree row changes that target's local hover styling even when the capture backend omits the cursor. The checker sees target-local change, sees no change in its unrelated top-left control crop, and reports a pass. Repeated or nearby targets also commonly become `indecisive`; the checker still returns `PASSED` if only one probe passes and all remaining probes are indecisive.

acceptance.statement: A recording with no cursor pixels but a target-local hover change must fail, every required click must be conclusively measured before the run can pass, and frame timestamps must be synchronized from an actual recording-start/end anchor rather than an unrelated last event.

issues.description:

- **Severity:** Major

- **Failure scenario:** An operator starts a real Dabbler session in an ordinary shipped VS Code window and needs one recording spanning `start_session` through `close_session`. The only recorder shown is still a Playwright scenario driver launching an Extension Development Host; `speed_ramp.py` only post-processes an already-existing recording. There is no observe-only start/stop entrypoint for the required human session.
- **Acceptance criterion:** `JUDGMENT - A documented harness must start and stop one recording around a manually driven session in an ordinary VS Code window, name it by set and session, avoid all session-state/orchestrator writes, and feed the resulting file and recorded start time into the speed-ramp workflow.`
- **Details:** **Violation:** Step 3 requires capture “around a real session in a real VS Code window, not the Extension Development Host,” and says the human replaces the scripted driver. **Impact:** The operator cannot execute the required recording workflow, so the “recordingPipeline” deliverable is incomplete regardless of the post-processing module. **Evidence:** `record-vscode-walkthrough.js` remains scenario-driven and launches the Extension Development Host; the measurement wrapper invokes that same recorder. No changed source provides a manual start/stop capture harness. The correct fix is a separate observe-only long-form recorder, not another scenario wrapper.

The only recorder shown is still a Playwright scenario driver launching an Extension Development Host; `speed_ramp.py` only post-processes an already-existing recording. The document explicitly says “Recording status: not yet recorded,” so the promised lifecycle demonstration cannot be watched or reproduced.

A reasonable reviewer cannot accept the session as complete. **Evidence:** The walkthrough is a proposed six-session outline and explicitly states that no recording has occurred. The diff contains neither the project/session sources nor recordings/ramp plans/safety decisions. The required source-rendered walkthrough is also replaced by a hand-authored document. The pointer blocker explains why recording stopped, but it does not satisfy the required deliverable.
